utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've asked for the witness to be kept out for a couple of minutes. The Court will remember that last week the present witness gave evidence of an entirely expert character for a portion of his evidence, touching on matters that had been dealt with by Court witness Helena Ranta. I sought and obtained the Court's leave to contact Dr. Ranta, and she very helpfully attended yesterday and is here today. Although a Court witness, we first of all asked her, she having been provided with a transcript, for any comments she had on the evidence that had been given and then sought her assistance a little more generally. I would ask that she be allowed to sit in court for the remainder of this part of the witness's evidence, fulfilling so far as is possible and appropriate, the functions of an expert able to advise Mr. Saxon, who will be asking questions of the witness, of any matters that she may regard as appropriate to be raised or that she may be able to assist him with. It's very good of her to have made her time available at such short notice to help the Court, and in light of the way things have developed, this would, in our respectful submission, be a useful and efficient way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Professor Ranta was -- Dr. Ranta was, of course, a Court witness rather than a Prosecution witness. The Court will remember it was an order of this Court which she fulfilled and gave evidence. So she is not allied to either party in this case, and we think it would be inappropriate that she adopted a position with the Prosecutor. She could, of course, be available for consultation by either party with the leave of the Court, but in our view it would be inappropriate for her to be sitting with the Prosecutor and acting, so to speak, as an instrument for him. If she is to fulfil such a function, she should be available for both sets of parties and not be in a position which allies her with one particular party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Ranta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, you can do however you decide. I don't mind one way or another. I would like to ask a question of a procedural nature before the witness comes in, please, so please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd simply -- in answer to Mr. Kay's point, if she's not able really to contact us and speak to us directly, it's going to become artificial and extremely slow. I sought your permission that we should speak to her over the weekend and in reality she has cooperated with us as an ordinary expert would, although as I explained to begin with, we asked her simply for her comments on the evidence. It's far easier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that's Mr. Kay's point, Mr. Nice. I think Mr. Kay's point is one of perception and availability in general. Whispering exchanges with Mr. Saxon in court, I don't think on the face of it is the right way to deal with a witness who is a Court witness. She should, on the face of it, be available to everyone for consultation, and I would be inclined to separate the issue of whether she should be present during the evidence of another witness from the one of where she should sit and be present, and that's how I intend to address it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure she would be prepared to speak to other parties in court, and if the Court insists that the consultation shall be a separate exercise from the giving of evidence, it will simply extend the process, but it's up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mrs. Ranta should sit in the public gallery, and she will be available to either party if they so wish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to what you said last time, I wished to ask that after Witness Dobricanin we have Witness Jasovic straight after him, and I'd just like to remind you, Mr. Robinson, that you said, and I'm reading this from the transcript, turning to me, "... if you wish to call [In English] that person as a witness, the person will be called at the earliest opportunity." [Interpretation] That's what you said, and this is the earliest opportunity, and I did have an opportunity, in keeping with your instructions, through the liaison officer to come into contact with the witness and to talk to him, and he's ready to testify, and this is the earliest opportunity after the ongoing witness. So I'd like you to give permission for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I object to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I object to the addition of this witness to the list of the accused's witnesses. That matter hasn't been dealt with. It's convenient for me to explain something through the Court to the accused, because he thought he made a point the last time we met about how it had been the Prosecution's decision to have this witness called. The accused often simply doesn't attend to procedural points or makes a point of not doing so and it's absolutely essential that he understands that what happened when he was notified of the presence of Jasovic in this building was one of the many examples of the Prosecution doing things to help this accused, a concern that he may not always, as a non-professional lawyer, be acquainted with things with which he might better be acquainted. So we simply told him about the presence here of that witness without in any sense suggesting that the witness should be called or without conceding that it would be right to call him. It would be quite wrong to call this witness who would be being called essentially - or this would have been the position - to produce three witness statements of some importance to the case because they would be witness statements going to suggest that people in Racak who died were members of the KLA when the Prosecution's case and evidence is to the contrary effect. There has still been no explanation given as to why witnesses should be called -- should not be called and why their statements should be given either hearsay or double hearsay. And it so happened that I was, over the weekend, looking at some earlier evidence, indeed the evidence of Mrs. Ranta -- or Dr. Ranta, and I happened upon an application by the accused to have evidence of statements of either Dunjic or Dobricanin read into the evidence in the course of that testimony, and His Honour Judge May -- I'll just find the point. I made a note of it -- made the observation then that it wasn't the practice for witness statements of individuals to be given when there was a procedure for producing them either within the Rules of the Tribunal or, of course, by calling the witness themselves. Our position in relation to these statements has been clear throughout from efforts -- despite efforts made to call them. It's our submission that the witnesses should come themselves to give evidence. There's no ground for calling such important evidence by hearsay, and accordingly that this evidence is now technically inadmissible at the hands of the man Jasovic. Let me just see if I can find the reference that I had over the weekend. Yes. It's on page 17762, where in answer to the accused Judge May said: "Our usual rule and one which I would have thought applied here is that we don't admit witness statement unless under particular Rules." He said of that particular proposed witness statement: "If you want to call these witnesses to give their evidence, you can do so, but uncross-examined material is not usually admitted." Further, I understand from a file I've been now provided with, coming from the Defence, that through Jasovic they now want to produce no less than something like 80 witness statements that I can show to you, all of which are untranslated. If these witness statements go to material matters in the Defence case, the witnesses should be called. If the Chamber were to decide that it would be appropriate, notwithstanding our argument to the contrary, to allow the material to be given in hearsay, it would plainly all have to be investigated and it would all have to be investigated before the witness comes to give his evidence. So I have two objections: First, there is no grounds for adding this witness's name to the Defence witness list; second, the evidence in principle that he wishes to call is evidence that is inadmissible because it's of an important nature and should come live from the witnesses concerned; and third as part of number two, I'm simply not in any position to deal with that material at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, are you then saying that Rule 92 bis and 89(F) are exhaustive as to the circumstances in which witness statements can be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think I can say that despite the fact that it was an observation from the Bench from your brother His Honour Judge Kwon that that topic was raised. I don't think I can say they are exhaustive because the provisions of general admissibility of hearsay are probably broader, or in the terminology that we sometimes use, would trump any restricting or implied restriction coming from 89(F) and 92 bis. What I can say is that in practice this Court has required important evidence from identifiable and living witnesses to be given live - Jovic is an absolutely standard example - and would require the necessary indicia of reliability to satisfy Rule 92 in the case of witness ill, deponents or statement makers who are dead, and His Honour Judge May's observation in the course of the Ranta evidence is one of a number of exemplifications of that general practice. Now, here this evidence is plainly potentially important, or it may be very important to the Racak case or the Racak count and the Racak part of the history, and there has been no inquiry made by the accused as to whether these witnesses are available, it appears, no effort made to call them, no effort made to see whether the statements allegedly given to a police officer are statements they currently adopt, and so on. This is material that should come live from the witnesses. There's no grounds, under your practice or under the Rules specifically, for it coming in the form of either the secondhand hearsay that it came in through the last witness or in firsthand hearsay as proposed through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is the criterion that the evidence is important or that it goes to the acts and conduct of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would have suggested that it's the former, not the latter, because there have been plenty of other requirements that witnesses come like Jovic. I mean, Jovic obviously goes in large part to the acts and conduct of the accused but he also goes to a whole lot of other matters as well and there was a general requirement that he should come along and give his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The point really is that if you follow 92 bis, if it goes to the acts and conduct of the accused, then the statement would not be admissible, and if in any event it raises an issue between the parties, then the witness should be available for cross-examination. Under 89(F), the witness is to be available for cross-examination. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's worth going back as to the reason why these statements were produced. They were produced by the witness showing the file that she had investigating the circumstances concerning the killings at Racak. They were relative and probative to that issue, and they were documents that she relied upon. Not to have produced such evidentiary material would have made a nonsense for the reason that the witness was giving evidence in the first place, and it was perfectly admissible, probative and relevant and went to the issues of which she was speaking. This matter now arises, in fact, because of cross-examination by the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber will remember that Mr. Nice alleged to the witness that the statements of three of the witnesses signed by the man Jasovic had been taken in circumstances of oppression and bad faith and conduct that was unacceptable. He went further and put allegations to the witness herself that she was aware of such oppressive techniques being used by police officers, was happy to condone it, and that was the whole circumstance, as he saw it, the Prosecutor saw it, behind the investigation of matters such as Racak and other important incidents of killings. Having put those allegations, Mr. Nice sought to adduce evidence in various forms, video evidence of interviews in which those allegations were made, and it so happened that Mr. Jasovic, who was the interviewing officer of those three particular witnesses, was acting as a Prosecution witness at the time. It is plainly correct and proper for an accused to be able to meet such serious allegations by calling that witness himself to deal with properly with the matters that should be put to him as a way of Mr. Nice being able to put his case and that witness being able to deal with the case that is being made. There is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What about the statements, the statements that the accused is seeking to have admitted through Mr. Jasovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I deal with that as a secondary issue, as the primary issue concerns Mr. Jasovic as he arose in cross-examination and as he arose in circumstances when none of us were aware of any significance of that name until the morning that Mr. Nice raised it and we spotted his name in the translations at the end of each statement. He is a Prosecution witness. The Prosecution have taken statements from him, called him as a witness in this building, are aware of the materials that have been thus far produced through the witness Marinkovic, and are perfectly able to deal with him if the accused chooses to call him. On the separate issue of the production of a further series of statements through that witness, I don't have any instructions upon that so I can't assist the Court any further. It's not something that has been brought to my attention. We are aware that in the Rule 68 material, because we researched it and provided it, that there are other statements that have been recorded by this witness Jasovic and that they're within the system. How it's to be used we don't know as of yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know if Judge Robinson intended this or not, but I thought the question extended to the three statements as well. And are you accepting that their relevance and probative value is confined to demonstrating what was in the possession, or the information in the possession of Judge Marinkovic at the time of the investigation and therefore the material in the possession of the authorities of the government in the most general sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. This is a two-stage matter, as I've viewed it, and I haven't been made privy to any information to the contrary that we're dealing with the matter concerning the allegations against Judge Marinkovic, which as I say perfectly proper for that witness to be used by the Defence. And the other issue would need further disclosure and perhaps an application to add the witness to the witness list if he's to deal with a far wider ambit of material so that there is disclosure between the parties of the relevant exhibits, there are translations and the matter can be considered for what it's worth. But at this stage, I'm not in a position to address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Milosevic, anything in reply?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Mr. Jasovic is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. testifying. I talked to him. I saw all the documents that he has with him at present, and he will testify about the statements that he took over a long period of time - relative, of course, relatively long - in 1998 and 1999. And all those statements were taken in keeping with the laws governing the Ministry of the Interior and him as an inspector, an investigator, and another inspector as well. They were signed by them, they were signed by the people giving the statements, so you can see how he went about the business of taking statements. Second, I think it is very useful, and I didn't know this because I had no idea that the witness existed, it's a very good idea to see that in these statements there is a lot of information which indicates, or at least partially indicates some things and information that the organs of the interior had about the activities of terrorists in the area of the village of Racak, Petrovo, Mala Poljce [phoen], Rana [phoen], it's all a very small area, in fact, and how all this took place. And among other things, in a large number of the statements that he gathered, that he collected in 1998 and 1999 before the event ever took place, before the police intervened in Racak at all, which shows us that there were different names in many of the statements, different names of persons who fell casualty in Racak. So by putting together all these pieces of information, you can paint a very clear picture about what actually happened and I think it is very useful for this witness to testify. And I realised that when you told me that I could talk to him and that you informed me that he could appear at the earliest opportunity, the person will be called at the earliest opportunity, as you said, I went ahead and I really did do my best to have it done at the earliest opportunity. And since the witness is testifying about his own work, what he did and the statements he himself took, so they're only statements taken by him personally, not the statements of some third party but him and his colleague, and indeed they signed the statements as investigators, you will find a great deal of information which is highly beneficial for understanding everything that took place. So I do appeal to you to give the go-ahead for him to testify after Witness Dobricanin. You will gain a clear picture. Judge Marinkovic testified. Jasovic will be testifying. Dobricanin has testified and is testifying, and you'll be given a very comprehensive, clear picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll give our decision -- we'll give our decision on this first thing tomorrow morning. We'll give our decision on your application tomorrow morning. The witness should, of course, in the meantime remain in The Hague. Let Dr. Dobricanin be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, we finished with your explanations regarding the paraffin glove. Now I would just like to put a few more questions to you that have to do with your observations, of course, if any. You noticed that on one of the pictures from the mosque that was made while the bodies were still there women can be seen wearing black clothes, in mourning. You had been in Kosovo for a long time. You are aware of the customs and habits there. Is there anything that seems strange to you in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that photograph before as I was surfing the Internet. I found it there, and I found it a bit strange due to two reasons. First of all, women, Muslim women do not enter mosques. Secondly, black -- the colour black is not the colour of mourning in the case of Muslims, and that surprised me a bit, and I have no explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Professor. Since we went through many aspects of everything that you looked into, in terms of what you saw on site and in terms of your own professional work in respect of all the dead, I would like to ask you now, bearing in mind all these questions, to go through some of the elements of 66(A), which says, inter alia: "After the shelling, the forces of the FRY and Serbia entered the village later in the morning and began conducting house-to-house searches. Villagers who attempted to flee from the forces of the FRY and Serbia..." All of that is in 66(a). And then there is this group of 25 men who attempted to hide in a building but were discovered by the forces of the FRY and the police. This is yet another allegation contained therein. Then it says that they were beaten and then were removed to a nearby hill where they were shot and killed, and so on and so forth. Professor, you said here that you were in Racak and that there were no signs of shelling there. Had there been any shelling, could it be assumed that you would have seen some traces of it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw no traces or signs of shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Professor. Had there been any shelling, let's look at it from yet another aspect, and then first shelling, as they say here, and then entering the village. Could it be assumed that the villagers would seek shelter from shelling? They would not wait there for the, as it says here, forces of the FRY and Serbia to enter the village. Is that a logical assumption?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, that's a normal reaction on the part of people who were attacked by any armed formation. They would probably flee from the village and seek shelter somewhere in order to be safe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, had there been any shelling, can it be assumed that somebody would have been killed from a shell?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Out of the 40 bodies from Racak, we did not find any traces on any of them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not helpful. It's not helpful to ask him whether it can be assumed that somebody would have been killed from a shell. It doesn't advance the matter one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. My question to him would have been whether there were any traces of wounds from shelling, and Professor Dobricanin said that the answer was negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it says in paragraph 66 that villagers were shot throughout the village as they were fleeing. So they were being targeted. So if they were targeted, it can be assumed that somebody would have been hit in the lower part of the body.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, again that's leading. "Can it be assumed..." Once you start in that way, you're leading. Get the evidence which this witness can give. You have been over this ground already with the witness. You're repeating yourself. Move on to other new areas.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right, Mr. Robinson. I just wanted to establish this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were no wounds in the lower part of the body. Everything was in the upper part of the body. And we have already established that you saw trenches, and that is probably due to the fact that they had been in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have the very distinct impression that you are searching now for questions, and you're trying to finish with a flourish. I think you are going to run into trouble. If you don't have new questions to ask, we'll bring the examination-in-chief to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. Then I am not going to put any other questions to Professor Dobricanin about Racak. I hope that he gave a comprehensive picture of everything. In that case, I shall just deal with a few more matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, here in tab -- I mean, in order to save time, I am going to refer to all three tabs, in tabs 13, 14, and 15. Please take a look at tab 13. This is a paper of yours that was written after the bombing of a bus on a bridge when the bus was hit by a bomb. What is discussed here is the casualties from that incident or, rather, the bodies of those who could have been identified.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This happened on the 1st of May, 1999, in the village of Luzane on a bridge. This happened at 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this information that you provide here, from what you established here, you carried out a forensic examination of 36 casualties out of the total of 40 persons who were killed, because four were soldiers, and they could be identified, and they could be handed over to their families. So you tried to identify 36 of the victims. And I see that among the identified persons there were 18 ethnic Albanians and eight ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not manage to complete all of this, because later on you had no more time to make it possible to have everything done.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can just say that after us, my Albanian colleagues who worked with me and who remained in the institute managed to establish the identity of the remaining persons as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many persons were killed by this one single bomb that came from an aircraft? You say that an old man was seriously injured but that he succumbed to his wounds within a month.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's 40 victims altogether, all passengers on the bus.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the passengers on that bus got killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could not carry out a detailed identification because the temperature of that bomb was over 2000 degrees Centigrade.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the bodies were charred. There was not a single body that had not been charred totally or partially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, can you assist me by identifying the issue in the case that this relates to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean these questions, Mr. Bonomy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, this particular tab.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has to do with the proceedings instituted by the authorities and the professional organs, how they worked in cases when violent death was established. This is work that was invariably carried out on the orders of the investigating judge in the interests of the investigation, whenever violent death would be established. So this was regular procedure as far as the state authorities were concerned, as well as the professional organs that assisted the state authorities. That is what is contained in tabs 13, 14, and 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And which paragraph of the indictment was this investigation in relation to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no specific paragraph of the indictment that this refers to, but throughout the indictment there is reference to discrimination against Albanians, the killing of Albanians by Serb forces, and so on and so forth, whereas here in very concrete action taken by the authorities, that is to say the judiciary, the professional organs that worked there, it is obvious that there is no discrimination in any way in terms of the ethnic background of victims. Whenever there is violent death, the legally prescribed procedure is applied. This is, therefore, aimed to refute another false thesis, namely that the authorities did not work to the benefit of all or were, rather, working against a particular ethnic group. And that can be seen quite clearly, because in tab 14, you have general conclusions about a large number of cases, and in tab 15 -- I mean in tab 14 the investigating judge from Pec gave orders to act, whereas in tab 15 the investigating judge in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In Prizren, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you can see that all cases were treated equally whenever violent death was established, in terms of carrying out the investigation, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, Professor, is whether this was the regular way the authorities worked or, rather, the investigation organs that investigated the violent death of citizens.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was regular procedure, well established, that was applied in the war conflict in a single way. We would get orders from investigating judges, and we would carry out post-mortems and give them our findings regardless of whether it was Serbs or Albanians who were killed, policemen, civilians, members of the KLA, whoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want to consider the relevance of this, the issue raised by Judge Bonomy. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fairness to the accused, the Prosecution concedes that there may be some margin of relevance to this material related to the -- the accused's criminal responsibility under Article 7(3), the allegations of failure to prevent or failure to discipline persons that were responsible for these actions, and part of those charges would be whether proper procedures were carried out to investigate matters in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. He's showing that there was a system in place, a system that worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think a rational argument could be made. I'm not conceding that it's powerful evidence, I'm simply conceding that the argument could be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Obviously it must go on, but is there any allegation, any suggestion that the pathology services or the forensic sciences services of the country were not operating properly?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Certainly not in the indictment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I thought that that was an issue being advanced in relation to Racak, the investigating judge, and the tenor of the cross-examination there was a criticism of the system that was said to stretch up from the accused -- or stretch down from the accused through the system repeatedly made by Mr. Nice concerning the court services and obviously the investigative judge who closely works with the forensic science services. That would be allied to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll hear the evidence, but let us move through it as quickly as possible, Mr. Milosevic, these three tabs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this has to do not only with the work of forensic science services but this goes to show that they go into action upon the order of an investigative judge. And in all these documents you can see that the forensic services addresses itself to the investigative judge who had initially issued an order for certain forensic action to be taken in order to clarify issues in the proceedings before the judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Professor. Now, could you please reply and refer to all of these three tabs. Tell us, was this a regular, routine procedure, and did you take identical action in all of these three cases in terms of the investigation that you were apart of?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are absolutely right. Not once did we diverge from the rules of our profession. Our school uses tradition of European forensic science, German and French mostly, and we acted exclusively upon the orders of an investigative judge, never outside of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have no further questions for Professor Dobricanin on the issue of his testimony. However, if you would allow me, there is something beyond that that I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would like to raise. Mr. Nice submitted here some dozen reports showing the signature of Professor Dobricanin. Mr. Nice did that in cross-examination of Judge Marinkovic, and it had to do with the cases when Professor Dobricanin, together with some other colleagues, examined some prisoners, establishing light bodily injuries in all cases. Mr. Nice presented this, trying to establish that the prisoners in those cases were tortured. Therefore, I wanted Professor Dobricanin to cover these findings or to address these findings which had been sent to the investigative judge, Danica Marinkovic, by a member of the commission, Professor Dobricanin, Muharem Rama, and Tefik Gashi, all of them doctors, showing that in all cases but one they established only light bodily injuries. And I would like to ask a few questions of Professor Dobricanin. Would you allow me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution does not object to questioning on this matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may put the matter to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I would like the usher to give these documents to Professor Dobricanin to take a look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have, Professor, to read out the names or anything else. Just please take a look at these documents. These are several findings establishing in all cases light bodily injuries as you determined.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember vaguely these cases. However, I have these documents before me dating to December of 1994 when several persons were brought to us who allegedly, at least that's what we were told, had been beaten while in detention. In any case -- in every case where a death of an Albanian person occurred in the course of an investigation, I would always establish a multi-ethnic commission comprising both Serbs and Albanians, because I wanted to ensure that it would be objective. In this case as well we had two Albanian assistant professors. That was back in 1994. The two of them, together with me, examined each of these persons, asking them how they had been injured, how they had sustained injuries. We described these injuries in our findings, in our reports in a detailed manner, describing how these injuries could have been inflicted and we gave our opinion and qualification of these injuries. In all of these cases, and some of these persons I knew personally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me just clarify this. What you have put before the witness are documents tendered by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. These are the findings of the medical commission which were introduced into evidence by Mr. Nice, showing that some seven or eight prisoners had light bodily injuries, established by -- at least, that was established by this commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I see. We haven't yet decided on their admissibility. We are at a disadvantage in that we don't have the documents in front us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, by a marvelous coincidence, I believe the Prosecution might be able to provide you with some copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. This is one copy. Let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What is the specific question that you have now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The specific question is as follows: Did you establish at the time that any of these persons had been tortured while in prison?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly they had certain injuries which qualified as light bodily injuries which could have been sustained in many various ways but could have been also inflicted by certain action while in prison. These were haematomas of small size which could have been inflicted by pressure applied, and I cannot exclude any circumstances under which this could have been inflicted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Professor. Did you have in your experience, did you encounter cases of persons who had been abused while in prison and who were forced to give certain statements by inflicting light bodily injuries upon them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really, because I -- unless I was involved in investigating and examining, I didn't know of any such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were attorneys, were defence counsel called in to confirm any of these allegations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not contacted by anyone. It is possible that they contacted my Albanian colleagues who signed this report as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just let me clarify this. The doctor was himself not involved personally in the examination of any of these persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was. I was. This was a three-member commission. I did not go to court proceedings where perhaps some of this was challenged and so on. Maybe my Albanian colleagues did; however, I took part in all of the examinations and signed and am one of the signatories to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do some of these not refer to the use of blunt instruments against the individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour. Blunt instruments and fist pressure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any reference to fists where there is a reference to the blunt instrument? It's not my recollection but unfortunately I don't have the documents. They were for another witness, and we weren't told to bring them today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. On the ELMO it says "a heavy blow from a blunt heavy mechanical implement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is a "blunt heavy mechanical implement"? If that's not a stupid question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it isn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bluntness of a mechanical implement can suppose everything starting from an instrument itself, from the pressure of fingers, police batons, any kind of a pole, anything that can apply blunt force. And this is what we understand in forensic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are actually trying to tell me that that sentence includes pressure from fingers? Is that what you mean to include by that reference? I find that astonishing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. In accordance with our classification as we see the application of force, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, does this mean that you make a distinction between blunt and sharp objects? Everything that is not a sharp object, including fists and feet, is considered a blunt instrument?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. Milosevic. We in forensic sciences, not only in Serbia but elsewhere in the world, make a distinction between sharp objects, firearms, and blunt objects. So everything that is not sharp and which is not considered a weapon is classified as a blunt instrument, including the pressure of fists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The word "mechanical," Doctor, how would a finger fit into that category?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It falls under that category, Your Honour, because that's pressure. This is mechanical object. It's not a weapon, and it's not a sharp object but, rather, applies blunt pressure, force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll just take a moment to put my papers in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: While we're doing that, can we get the exhibits sorted out at the end of this so they go on the record? Tabs 13, 14, 15, 16 by my record haven't been officially entered into the trial proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The one under 12 is the same one as D2?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: D2, which has been marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. May 13 to 16 go in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And D2 should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now it's been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit D2, and then tabs 13, 14, 15, and 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon. Cross-examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will try -- I will do my best to pronounce your name correctly. I can't promise that I will do it always successfully, but I will try. Professor, one of the things that you said towards the end of your testimony on Friday of last week certainly resonated with me. You said, "I don't want to separate the people, the Albanians and the Serbs, because they both suffered a great deal in that war. It was a great misfortune." And I just want to take a moment now to ask you some questions, because it's my understanding that in your professional capacity since the events of 1999, you have been working in your own way to alleviate some of that misfortune, and what I mean by that is trying to exhume and identify persons who died in Kosovo in 1999. Is that -- is that a correct statement? You need to say a verbal answer.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fully accurate, yes. This is a fully correct statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair for us to assume here that because you and your office moved to a more northern region of Serbia after the events in 1999, that to continue with your medicolegal investigations in Kosovo you would have required assistance and cooperation from officials of UNMIK?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you recall, for example, when you had your first contacts and assistance from UNMIK officials in this respect, what year that was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I had contact with UNMIK and with their officials was, I think, in 2001 when there was a terrorist attack on the bus travelling between the administrative border in Merdari and Podujevo. Eleven persons were killed in that incident, and together with my colleagues I joined the UNMIK officials, who were of different ethnic background, to conduct the autopsy of the victims, which was done in the British hospital in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So beginning in 2001 and subsequently, you began to have contact and collaboration with UNMIK officials so that you could carry out this kind of forensic work within the province of Kosovo. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall what part of 2001 it was; the beginning of the year, end of the year, middle of the year?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly. That was in 2001, when via the commission of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia cooperation was established in this field together with my colleagues from UNMIK who were from different countries and my team consisting of my colleagues. We started working together on several exhumations. First of all, we examines several bodies which had already been examined -- exhumated. We did that in the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Pristina which is where I used to worked before. I'm sorry if my answer was too long. This cooperation was exceptional and is continuing to this day and continues to be very successful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And would the members of UNMIK also assist you if you needed records or documents that had been left behind, for example, in the Forensic Medical Institute in Pristina in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw those documents again. They just gave us documents which related to investigations into the killing of Serbs or other non-Albanians or Albanians dating to 1999. And the autopsy findings and reports that physicians had conducted that came in with core or perhaps The Hague investigators, but nothing apart from that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- well, when you requested assistance, let's say documentation or assistance in obtaining documentation from members of UNMIK, were you ever refused that assistance that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said a moment ago that there was a very high degree of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to also reflect for a few minutes on something that you said today, which I think is also quite clear from watching your testimony. Mr. Milosevic asked you whether you were familiar with the customs of the people of Kosovo. Do you recall that? That was just about an hour ago, a little bit less.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously, Professor, you were -- you were born in Kosovo, I believe. You grew up there. You studied there. You've had a long career there up until 1999. Well, your work continues there to this day, I realise. So can we understand that you would also have made, during your lifetime, many friends and colleagues of all ethnicities living in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I had neighbours and friends and colleagues who are Albanians. I worked with them and had very good cooperation with them, and I personally never had any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were familiar with their customs and traditions, the customs, traditions, way of life of the Albanian population, or at least those who were your friends?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke about the customs of the Albanian population in this case it was the custom of Muslim Albanians, not Catholic Albanians, Albanians who have different customs, perhaps. Yes, I was acquainted with both of them, both types, because I lived together with them for 46 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those 46 years, did you ever have a situation where you learned or you observed that one of your Albanian friends or colleagues was known by more than one name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not sure I'm following you. Could you answer the question or reformulate it? I don't know what you mean actually. I didn't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try to give you a more concrete example. For example, did you ever have a friend or colleague of Albanian ethnicity who might have had a particular name on his identity documents but was known by -- to you or to that person's friends by some other name, perhaps the person's father's name? Did you ever encounter such situations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I don't think I ever encountered a situation like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask your assistance with something, and I'm going to have to ask Mr. Prendergast's assistance as well. I'd like the witness to be shown a copy of Exhibit D291. For the benefit of the witness, this document was presented by Judge Marinkovic in the Cyrillic alphabet, so that would probably be of most use for Professor Dobricanin, but I believe we have some English copies for the other parties present. And perhaps if an English copy could be placed on the ELMO and turned to page -- and turned to page 2. Professor Dobricanin, this is a list of names prepared by someone you know, obviously, Danica Marinkovic. It's titled "List of identified bodies found in the village of Racak." And if you could, please, could you direct your attention on page 2 to names 32, 33, and 34, which are towards the bottom of the page in the English version, a little bit higher Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. up in the Serbian version. Do you see those names? The first name we see is Sukri Jasari. Number 33 is Raif Jasari, and number 34 is Jasar Jasari. Do you see those names?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now very briefly I'd like to show you an annex to the Prosecution's indictment in this case, because the Prosecution in this matter has also presented a list of names of persons who died at Racak. And I can provide an extra copy for the witness and/or the ELMO, and I'd ask that we turn to here page 43 of my copy. It's Schedule A to the Racak indictment. Do you have that list from the Prosecution next to you now, Professor Dobricanin? Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also see now, if we look about halfway down the page, we see the same names that I just read from Judge Marinkovic's list, the three Jashari relatives; Jasher Jashari, Raif Jashari, and Shukri Jashari. Do you see those?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can see that these three names are on both lists. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look just a little bit further down that same page, and further down that page there are two people with the name Salihu, first name Jasher and first name Shukri. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, if Mr. Prendergast could remove those lists for the time the time being because I need to use another document. I'd like to -- Ms. Dicklich, I'd like to show the statement of Rizah Salihu, if we can. And perhaps that statement could be placed on the ELMO as well for the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, I don't know how fluent you are in the English language but I'm going to read some parts of this out so you can certainly hear the interpretation in your own language as well. But this is a witness statement given to members of this Tribunal, the Office of the Prosecutor, by a man named Rizah Salihu. And if we turn to the statement itself, in paragraph 2 Mr. Salihu explains that he resides in the village of Racak, he is the eldest of six brothers, and that three of his brothers were killed in Racak on the 15th of January, 1999. And just below that he provides the names of his deceased brothers; Jashar Salihu, Raif Salihu, and Shukri Salihu. And if you can recall, we've seen those first names, Jashar, Raif, and Shukri already on both of the lists that I showed you a few minutes ago, only with the surname Jashari. And then in paragraph 3, Mr. Salihu explains that at birth his brothers were given the family name of Salihu. But in paragraph 4, he explains that he had an uncle named Jashar Salihu, and that sometimes persons in the village of Racak refer to members of his family with the last name Jashari. And he explains in paragraph 5 that when the bodies of his brothers were found in January of 1999, that someone incorrectly identified his three brothers with the surname Jashari. And if I can, he also says in paragraph 7 that the markers on his brothers' graves bear the family name of Salihu.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if I can have the first batch of photographs, please. If I may very quickly bother Mr. Prendergast again, and if these three photographs could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are three photographs which I took in the cemetery at Racak about ten days ago. The first one shows the name Jashar Salihu. The second one shows the name Raif Salihu. And the third one shows the name Shukri Salihu.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the brother in this statement also explains that he has provided copies of the death certificates for his brothers with the surname Salihu. Now, I know you lived in Kosovo for many years, and you're familiar now with the two different lists of names that I've showed you, Professor Dobricanin, one created by Judge Marinkovic, another one created by the Office of the Prosecutor. Can we agree right now that a mistake was made in both lists, that where the names -- where the surname says Jashari, Jashar, Raif, and Shukri, on both lists that is actually incorrect, or at a minimum not the most accurate name? Do you agree with me on that, what I've just shown you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, please, Judge Robinson, might I be allowed to give an explanation by way of two or three sentences with respect to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the forensic team, we did not take part in the final identification. That was done by the crime technicians. And we know that with all 40 bodies in Racak, that all 40 bodies, 37 were identified of the 40 bodies, and I think that the mix-up came with these three people, that they are in fact the same people. But what is very important and what we kept saying, and we've been discussing that, we didn't make a separate conclusion, three individuals that were autopsied from the village of Racak were not circumcised. They were not circumcised, which is the custom with all Muslims in the world, including Albanian Muslims in Kosovo and Metohija. So I am afraid that those three bodies were intentionally or unintentionally during this process of identification, because they weren't all identified, they were identified on the basis of ID identification documents and fingerprints or because their relatives recognised them or not, that those three bodies were taken away and buried in other place, where as the three brothers Jashari, who of course would be buried in their village in their family graveyard, have been buried under these three -- the three pictures. It's just my statement that we found three persons, three corpses who were not circumcised, which means that they were not Muslims, so that might be an explanation, and I apologise for taking up more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Saxon, does it follow from that list that you have got two bodies too many on your list?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There is more to go in this process, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, dear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- which I am trying to clarify. So with great respect, I would prefer not to answer your question right at this moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, at no time did I mean to imply that you had committed any error regarding identification. That was not my intention at all. I was simply trying to clarify the names, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You will recall, Judge Bonomy, that Judge Marinkovic referred to discrepancies in the different lists and I'm simply trying to clarify these discrepancies, that's all. Mr. Prendergast, if once more we could place on the ELMO the list -- it's D291, the list provided by Judge Marinkovic. And if that could be turned to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Professor Dobricanin, if you could simply direct your attention to what's referred to as body number 37. Do you see that? And the name --

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Syla Sabri. It's surname Syla and then --

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Syla, Syla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me. So the first name would be Sabri and the surname would be Syla.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Prendergast, if you could replace Judge Marinkovic's list with Schedule A from the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Professor Dobricanin, if you look down that list, you don't see anybody with the name Sabri Syla, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's Syla Sheremet and Syla Shyqeri.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But no Syla Sabri, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be an appropriate time to take the morning break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, thank you, Mr. Saxon. We'll take the break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, just before we took the break -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before we took the break, we established that nowhere on Schedule A to the Prosecution's indictment do we find the name Sabri Syla or Sabri Sulja or Syla; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I could have Mr. Prendergast's assistance again, if we could distribute the statement of Milazim Syla. And if a copy could be placed on the ELMO, please. This is a statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor by Mr. Milazim Syla or Sulja. He is also a resident of Racak. Paragraph 2 he tells us that in 1999, he was a member of the Kosovo Liberation Army, but on the 15th of January, he was not in Racak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then turning to paragraph 3, Professor Dobricanin, he says that the following members of my family were killed in Racak on the 15th of January: Sabri Syla or Sulja, who was the father of the declarant; Haki Metushi, his uncle; Arif Metushi, another uncle; and Sahide Metushi, his aunt. And then in paragraph 5 Mr. Syla explains that at birth his father and his brothers were given the surname Syla or Sulja but during the 1980s his uncles decided to change their family name, their surname to that of Metushi, following a tradition in their family. In paragraph 6, however, it is explained that at that time the father of the declarant, Sabri Syla, was working in Macedonia, and he was unable to change his surname. And when he returned from Macedonia to Kosovo, he also felt unable to change his surname formally from Syla to Metushi. In paragraph 7, it remarks that the father of this declarant is buried with his brothers in a cemetery in Racak in a grave bearing the name Sabri Metushi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would just like again to ask Mr. Prendergast's assistance if we could put a photograph -- actually, three photographs on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see the first photograph of brother Arif Metushi. Next photograph, please. And then the photograph of Sabri Metushi, who was the father of this declarant, also known as Sabri Syla. And Haki Metushi. We also see in the last paragraph, paragraph 9, that attached to the statement is a copy of the licna karta of Sabri Syla and hence that name being found on the list of -- produced by Judge Marinkovic. Could we look again, please, at Schedule A to the indictment. And Professor Dobricanin, if you go down that list you'll see, sort of in the lower half of that list, we see the two names Arif Metushi, Haki Metushi, but nowhere do we see their brother Sabri Metushi, also known as Sabri Syla. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's probably as you say, but I'd like to draw your attention to this: I have absolutely no knowledge about any of these names. While we conducted the autopsies at the institute, we didn't receive the names of those who had been killed nor were we interested in that because those people had been transferred to the mortuary, the process of identification had been carried out, and the documents were taken to the crime technology department of the district SUP. All I can say is I came across these names here and nowhere else so I really can't say. I don't know. I don't know why you're asking me this in the first place when I know nothing about this. I don't know the names. I don't know these -- well, these queries as to whether it's one person or another, I really can't say anything because I don't know, and this is the first time that I'm seeing these names here and the documents. We conducted the autopsies, the identification process took place in another premises, in different rooms, so I don't know about that. Later on, they might have sent me the -- something that I never received -- a document for checking out the names, but I never received that so I really have no idea about why you're asking me this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, is the name Sabri Syla on Judge Marinkovic's list?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where would I find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You will find it, Your Honour, at number 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 37, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you this question, Professor Dobricanin, simply because of your long-standing knowledge of Albanian culture. That's why I'm asking you these questions, simply to help us clarify these points. That's all.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to say something very briefly to assist you, if I can, because I'm a little confused about all this. There are Albanian families whose members have different surnames. Not only with Albanians. There are parts of Kosovo where Serbs changed their surnames and then you have the case where two brothers don't have the same surname. It's probably a vestige of the age-old culture that developed alongside each other over the centuries. The next point is that when somebody, when an Albanian -- we had occasion to see this -- comes to recognise somebody or identifies, he might say, let's say, Miftar Banushi, whereas Banushi is not the surname, it is Miftar and the father's name is Banushi. So perhaps this is what this is all about; instead of us giving a surname, they say Salihu Jashari or Jahsarit which means Sali of father Jashari. So maybe that's what's caused this confusion, where the father's name is given rather than the surname. So possibly that was the source of the confusion, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Professor Dobricanin. I don't want to bore you with this or the other members of the Court. I'm only going to discuss with you one more name and then we'll move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this -- is this something that the witness can actually specifically deal with? I mean, he's said what he knows. Is this not legal argument now or argument on the facts as they are contained in the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution believes, Your Honour, that because of this witness's knowledge of Albanian culture, and as he pointed out, the local Serbian culture, and given his recent -- his -- the response that he just gave, he can certainly confirm that this confusion is, quite frankly, fairly common in the culture where he resided for so many years, and we're simply trying to explain why there are discrepancies on this list. Your Honour, to save time, what I would like to produce for the Chamber is an aide-memoire. And I'd ask that this be marked as an exhibit, please. And if a copy of this could be placed on the ELMO. Your Honours, this is simply a simple chart which the Prosecution has created that describes -- that -- with a list in the far left column of the names in Schedule A to the indictment, and in the remaining columns evidence that the Prosecution has obtained regarding, for some of these people, the use of other names and/or other surnames. And I would offer this as an aide to the Trial Chamber, and of course we will -- we do Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. intend to make a written submission in the near future regarding this issue and offering for the Chamber a revised list of names to correspond to the Racak part of the indictment. With a represented accused or an accused who would have been more cooperative, we would have tried to negotiate this, but we felt that that was not appropriate in this case, in the circumstances of this case. If you have no questions on this, then I will move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps it should be a filing to amend the indictment. That's really what it comes down to, that the names within Schedule A have been duplicated and names omitted, and perhaps the appropriate course is to make a filing on that matter and give the explanation as to the history of this matter as based upon the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, are there examples of the Prosecution actually writing to the accused seeking specific agreement on matters and making no headway? Because if there aren't, then why don't you submit it to him, refer to the discussion in court, and ask if it can be agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been working on this case since the accused was detained in the summer of 2001. I am not aware of any indication by this accused since that time that he would be willing to even communicate with members of the Office of the Prosecution. I may be wrong, because a lot of time has passed, but that is my impression. Perhaps Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you're turning the matter on its head that way, Mr. Saxon. I appreciate the problem, don't misunderstand that, but if you have something that you want to specifically have agreed, then it may be worth trying. You can't really lose anything by at least trying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Point well taken, Your Honour, and we will follow the appropriate channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, next topic, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, I'd like to move on to some questions that I have about your testimony from last week, and I guess first of all, since several days have passed by, you may have had some time to think about your comments here during two days last week. Is there anything that you want to change, amend, or modify?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not have anything to add or to take away. Perhaps some of the wording could have been clearer, but do I not recall having said anything that was unclear. I don't wish to add anything, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If Mr. Prendergast could show to -- perhaps Professor Dobricanin already has it with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to turn your mind to tab 6 of your exhibits. This was the general conclusions provided by the Yugoslav team of expert forensic scientists on the 30th of January, 1999, to Judge Danica Marinkovic. Do you have it there in front of you, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could focus your attention on the very last paragraph, paragraph 14, where in English it says: "It should be stressed that the work of all forensic experts involved in this forensic effort was performed at a high professional level and with full mutual respect and confidence." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at least as of January the 30th, 1999, you had no problems or criticisms to make about Dr. Helena Ranta, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did not. I had an excellent cooperation with her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we turn now to tab 11, which were the comments made at a press conference by Dr. Ranta on the 17th of March, 1999, and if we turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ah, yes. This was also Exhibit C1, Your Honours. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, we see in the last sentence of the first paragraph, the sentence says: "There were no indications of the people being other than unarmed civilians." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And clearly you and your colleagues did not -- you and your Yugoslav colleagues, I should say, did not agree with that sentence, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not agree with that sentence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the -- the problems, if I can use that term, regarding the work of Dr. Ranta arose on the 17th of March, 1999, with that sentence in this press conference; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that was one of our objections to what our colleague Dr. Helena Ranta had to say. With your permission, I could explain why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we already understand why, Professor Dobricanin. If you turn, please, to tab 3.1. Actually, I apologise, tab 3 first. You mentioned in your testimony last week that there were disagreements between Dr. Ranta and the other members of the Finnish forensic team regarding the results of the work done concerning the events at Racak. Tab 3 is an article published in Forensic Science International in February of 2001. It's one of the articles that you presented. Is there anything that you disagree with in this article?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is absolutely nothing in here that I would disagree with. This is an article about our joint work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you see -- can you tell us where in this article there is a mention of a disagreement with Helena Ranta?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the English version in front of me. I don't speak English very well, but never mind. I don't think that there is very pronounced disagreement, but I believe that forensic scientists should not speak about the origins, about what had happened there where the bodies had been found. I think that is the only disagreement. I mean, whether it's disagreement or not is for them to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, Dr. Dobricanin, that during your testimony last week you were not speaking about what happened in Racak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please rephrase your question. I did not understand it. Could you please ask me again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you just told the Chamber -- you said, "I don't think there is very pronounced disagreement." So we've clarified that. "But I believe that forensic scientists should not speak about the origins, about what had happened there where the bodies had been found." Now, don't you think last Thursday and Friday when you were testifying before this Chamber you were doing exactly that? You were giving your opinion - I should say opinions - about what happened in Racak on the 15th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I could not have presented such an opinion according to any criteria. Had they allowed me into Racak on the 15th of January, you would have a much more definitive answer in this regard today. I just said once when one of Their Honours asked me why I emphasised this, I said that -- I mean, when asked why this was not an execution, I gave some of my own explanations. That is the only thing that I said in relation to the events in Racak. I'd never say anything about what had happened in Racak except for what I saw myself. Nothing would give me the right to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So I will move on. If we look in paragraph 4, we see the following sentence: "Forensic pathologists can determine the cause and manner of death --" this is on page 8 -- "and note other injuries, pathological changes, and facts for identification. Determination of reasons for events, their political and moral meanings or the connection of victims to political or other organisations are questions which lie beyond the scope of forensic science. This should be realised by the authorities and also by the forensic scientists themselves." Now, your comments last week about the connection of some of the victims or all of the victims in Racak to certain organisations such as, for example, so-called Village Guard, would fall into this category, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question put to me was to explain why there were several layers of clothing and what I saw then in Kosovo. I gave my opinion not as a specialist in forensic medicine but as a person who is quite familiar with the circumstances under which all of this happened, because I was on the move all the time, I was travelling all the time because of different autopsies in the area, and nothing more than that. What we did in the Institute for Forensic Medicine in terms of autopsy led to all our other conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
