utterances.text: So just to clarify, Professor, when you say, "I gave my opinion not as a specialist in forensic medicine," so can we understand, then, today that the opinions that you gave last week about the possible scenario of events in Racak on the 15th of January, 1999, were not based on your expertise as a forensic scientist? It was simply your opinion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment when I saw the bodies in the mosque in Racak, and after that when I saw the bodies in our institute, that is to say everything I saw as a citizen who was going through the village and also as a member of the investigation team that toured the trenches under fire, I said as a member of the investigation team. Everything I said about the bodies I said as a professor and a specialist in forensic medicine. Those are two things that have to be distinguished between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you for that distinction. By the way, at one point in your testimony last week, you mentioned -- I know you said today, a little while ago, that there were no strong or profound disagreements between Dr. Ranta and the other members of the Finnish team, but last week you mentioned that the Finns had published a report, that Dr. Ranta's colleagues had published a report somewhere, and Judge Bonomy asked you, well, what report? Where was it published? Can you tell us where we can find this report? And you weren't able to provide a very specific response at that time. Have you had any time to think about that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that I said that they published it. I told you that I heard about it somewhere or saw it somewhere. Now, where this was, I don't know. Perhaps it was in a discussion that we had at the institute. We discussed everything there as colleagues at the institute. We were all thinking about this. We were all wondering how we could explain the positions of all those wounds in the case of persons who had multiple wounds. And then at that moment we said that this did not look like execution, that it did not look like execution. We are not eyewitnesses of these events. I'm not an eyewitness either. A forensic doctor speaks with greater or lesser probability about events than caused such-and-such wounds, and that is how you have to understand this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, you used the pronoun "we." You said, "We discussed everything there as colleagues. We were all thinking about this. We were all wondering. And then at that moment we said that this did not look like execution." Now, are you including members of the Finnish -- or I should say the European Union team when you used the pronoun "we" here; and if so, could you please tell us which members of the Finnish team?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not say that we said that it had not been an execution but that it had not looked like an execution. All the members of the team, the Serb, Finnish, Belorussian, we talked, we had discussions, we had breaks, we chatted as friends and colleagues, and we talked about all the possibilities, because not all of us -- or, rather, until the present day I do not understand how we could explain each and every one of these wounds. It's only natural. We say "in all likelihood," "it is likely," or whatever, but we cannot establish that with 100 per cent certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, just one more question on this and then hopefully I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, did you get the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, no. I'm following up on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name a specific member, an individual member of the Finnish forensic team who specifically agreed with your conclusion that what happened to the people in Racak did not look like an execution? Can you name one member of that team?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot give you any names of any member of the team, either the Finnish team or our team. It's been many years. It was just a discussion that we had, a chat, either within the autopsy room or outside it. I really can't say anything to you at this stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. It's been many years. Let's take a look, if we can, Professor, at tab 12 of your exhibits. Tab 12 is an article written by you, Professor Dobricanin, and three of your colleagues. And I'd like to ask you to direct your attention to what is page 13 in the English version. And a little ways down the page, page 13, you and your colleagues begin to discuss Helena Ranta, the Finnish forensic expert team leader, and I believe you're making a reference to what is tab 11, the press conference from the 17th of March, 1999, and this is what you say in the English translation: "Using the political and not medical terminology, Dr. Ranta condemns Serbs for massacre of the innocent, unarmed civilians ..." Then it goes on to explaining that the diphenylamine is not sure, et cetera, et cetera. Do you see that, Professor Dobricanin? Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn back, now, to the previous tab, tab 11. And this is the text of Dr. Ranta's comments made at the press conference on the 17th of March. And can you tell us, please, where in these comments Dr. Ranta condemns Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there are direct and indirect indicators about the things that were referred to in my professional article. If we say that this document is, in terms of its title, a report of the forensic professional team of the EU about the events in Racak, in the first paragraph it says that the comments constitute a personal view of the authors. Then it is obvious that these are not comments made by the EU team or the Finnish team but simply comments made by Ms. Helena Ranta. That is what she is saying, and that's the only thing I said. I made no other comment. She says and concludes that -- yes, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought I asked a direct, simple question. The question was simply this --

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- where in the comments of Dr. Ranta does Dr. Ranta condemn Serbs for the events that occurred in Racak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no such sentence. I did not find that sentence in her comment, and I'm sure that that sentence would not belong in these comments. But the indirect detrimental consequence of such an opinion was the beginning of the bombing of Serbia and Montenegro at the time. The very words that these were unarmed civilians, that means that this was a brutal killing, and these victims were found in a gully, et cetera, et cetera, and we cannot have any information about that, we were not eyewitnesses, neither Mrs. Ranta nor I. That shows that there was acceptance of an opinion that this was some kind of retaliation against the Albanian population of the village of Racak. I gave a detailed explanation as regards the text -- the test that is called the paraffin test, and if there are any further clarifications that are required, I'm prepared to give them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are some, Professor Dobricanin. I think you just acknowledged that in a professional article that you published under your name, you said something untrue about another professional colleague. Do you think that is responsible? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say anything that was untrue. I just commented on the fact that forensic doctors are not supposed to give political comments that could lead to a very serious reaction on the part of the international public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, can you turn back to tab 12, please. Page 13 of the English version again. And if we look about halfway down the page, following the sentence that I read to you previously, we see the following sentence: "This kind of political and not thinking of the forensic doctor ended with opinion that there is no reason to believe that these individuals are the members of the terrorist organisation KLA." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we turn back to tab 11, Dr. Ranta's comments, where at the end of Dr. Ranta's comments do you find such an opinion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it on page 4, paragraph 2 in the last sentence. "There were no indications that these were persons who could be anything but unarmed civilians." She did not have the right to state that. She did not have any proof for any such thing. And we, all together, her team and our team, had indirect proof that these people had gunpowder particles on their hands -- sorry, nitrate particles on their hands. That is what we can talk about. But we did not have any additional documents, any findings that they were unarmed civilians. This was not a forensic medical qualification of something that happened there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on, Professor Dobricanin, to the events of Racak, and I'm going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I be clear about one thing, Mr. Saxon? I probably should know but I've forgotten. Did Dr. Ranta accept that the paraffin glove test had produced the results which were claimed for it? By that I mean the physical results. What conclusion you draw from it is another matter, but that one of four possible causes existed for the results that were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe the answer to that question, Your Honour, is no, because it's my understanding that any such results were never provided to the members of the Finnish team, that the -- whatever paraffin or gunpowder residue tests were made were taken before the arrival of the group of Finnish experts. Obviously Dr. Ranta could provide you with a more specific response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness knows the answer. Professor Dobricanin, were the European Union forensic team given the details of the results that were found by the technicians who carried out the paraffin glove test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that they were given that. I'm not sure, but I don't think that they received it, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, if I could just try to summarise some of the evidence that you gave last week regarding the events in Racak. You provided your opinion - I understand it's only now an opinion as a citizen - that the victims in Racak were killed in some kind of combat situation, and you based that opinion, if I understood your testimony correctly, on four factors, and let me just explain my understanding of them so that we can discuss it. The first factor was the fact that the victims wore several layers of clothing. The second factor was that many of the victims wore clothing that was dark in colour. The third factor were the results of the gunpowder residue tests. And the fourth factor were the fact that the bodies exhibited different bullet paths. In other words, bullets that impacted on the bodies but coming from different directions. Is that a fair summary of your testimony on this issue?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. For right now, I'd like to show a bit of video, if I may. And you also recall that you testified that you saw no damage to any of the houses at Racak when you went there. Let's look at this video first. I believe this is from the 17th of January, the first clip that we're going to see. This video comes from the material that Judge Danica Marinkovic presented during her testimony here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here we see a trench line in the woods. A shovel. Can we stop it right there for a moment? Professor Dobricanin, I believe that is you, isn't it, crouching between those two cars? Is that you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Please correct me if I'm wrong. I think this was the 17th of January. Obviously it's wintertime. You're dressed warmly, are you not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had only one jacket, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Were you naked underneath that jacket?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you wearing on that day underneath your jacket?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I wore a sweater and a winter shirt. I'm not sure. I know that I always wore this jacket when going out to work in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you're wearing this jacket, you're wearing a sweater, you're wearing a winter shirt. Any undershirt, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you made a mistake. I said that I had a jacket, a sweater, or a winter or a thick shirt, not both of them. I normally wear just that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. My mistake if I misunderstood you. It might have been a mistake in translation. The point I'm simply trying to make is that you were wearing more than one layer of clothing on that day, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take the vest into account and a shirt, then certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now -- and can I assume that the person with you who is wearing a nice blue winter parka also had some clothing on underneath the parka?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't examine that. I just saw a jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do have a lot of common sense. You're an intelligent man. You know that most people in the wintertime, when they go outside they put on their winter jacket, and they usually have something on underneath their jacket; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. They certainly do have it. It is sure that they do not put a jacket on a naked body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, should we draw particular conclusions from the fact that you and your colleague or colleagues wore more than one layer of clothing in January of 1999 in the Racak area besides the conclusion that it was cold?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you have in mind multi-layered clothing of the people who were killed in Racak, and if you plan to compare that with the clothing that we wore, these are two completely different things. Those people there had two jackets, several sweaters, several winter clothes, several pairs of socks, of trousers, and very good boots. What we had on is the clothes that we regularly wore; a jacket and perhaps a sweater or a shirt. We did not plan on spending a lot of time outside in the cold in low temperatures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, Professor Dobricanin. And I would like to compare the clothing that you wore, briefly, with the clothing found on the victims from Racak, because quite frankly, and I don't mean any disrespect by this, but you and your colleagues were probably in a different socio-economic place than the majority of the residents at Racak. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. I was not a wealthy man. I could not spend a lot of money on clothing or anything else. We lived on our salaries. I lived on my salary. That was the system we had. Many people in Albanian villages had other sources of income; agriculture, trade, and so on. Many of their children, brothers, and so on worked in foreign countries. Therefore, I don't think that you can compare the standard of all of these people. The first house that I had I acquired just ten months before being forced to flee Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And many of these people, many of these residents of the Racak area have relatives who live in Switzerland because there is little or no work in the Racak area except for subsistence farming. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That does not apply only to Albanians, sir. We were going through a very hard crisis. We lived under embargo. You know that sanctions had been introduced. So that did not apply only to Albanians but to Serbs in towns and villages. All of these people suffered a great deal because of everything that was lacking. And I am very familiar with this because I toured many Albanian villages as a physician. We had in the 1970s an epidemic of variolavera so I visited a lot of villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Dobricanin, I'm going to cut you off now. I think you've tried to answer my question. The point is this, though: If you're not a university professor, if you don't have a reliable income, if you're poor, you can't afford to buy the nice winter clothes that you and your colleague were wearing there on the 17th of January, if you have to go out in the wintertime, particularly early in the morning, you might put on a few layers of clothing, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I did not say that I was poor. As a university professor, my standard of living was certainly higher than many of those villagers. However, I was not rich to be able to spend money left and right. This -- I apologise for speaking about this, but this jacket was the jacket I wore when I went to work in the field because it was a warm jacket, it had a lot of pockets that could used for my notebooks and so on. Yesterday, in The Hague, I saw people sunbathing in the sun, whereas I wore a sweater and a jacket and didn't feel too warm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So yesterday you were also wearing more than one layer of clothing, but we shouldn't make any conclusions about your political associations based on that, should we?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm a man of a certain age. I like to wear warm clothes. I never walk out in only one layer of clothing except when I'm at the beach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Professor Dobricanin, I want to move on to the subject of the gunpowder residue test which we also referred to here as the paraffin test. Perhaps you can clarify one thing -- and now I realise that I have moved too quickly, so I have to interrupt my last thought. Can we move to the next video, to the Dobricanin 3, please. Dobricanin 2 and 3. Fine. We'll go to 3. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we stop right there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, this again is some video material submitted by Danica Marinkovic. It shows the Racak area. And do you see this part of a house here on the right-hand side? It appears to be a house that has been burnt out. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if you -- can you recall if you saw this house on the 17th of January when you visited the community?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw this site or anything similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we look at the remainder of this clip and then the next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we stop here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, this is a house in Racak. I believe it's the 17th of January. Might be the 18th, but no later than that. The house is still shouldering. Can you see the smoke rising?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it here on this picture, but I did not see it there at the site. And I would have seen it because I climbed to the highest elevation above Racak where the bunker was, and I never saw this. Did you say it was on the 17th? Not on the 17th. I did not see it. I was in Racak on the 18th, and I did not see it then either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what do you suppose happened to this house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This house was set on fire, is on fire. I couldn't tell you anything more about it. I don't know whether this house is located in Racak. But based on what we see, I cannot explain this. Perhaps this house was on the outskirts of the village, because I would have remembered had I seen this from the hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, it is possible, at least, that a house on the outskirts of the village of Racak was damaged by some kind of fire on the 15th of January, some type of gunfire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're asking me something that I truly don't know. I said even before that I am familiar with certain types of weapons, but I cannot identify the damage on the road, on the houses and tell you what weapon had caused it, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Professor. Let me move on now to the topic of gunpowder residue tests that were done. Can you -- can you clarify for us when the -- what day were these tests carried out on the 40 bodies that were brought from Racak to the morgue? Was it the 19th of January, the day the bodies were transported to the morgue, or was it some other day, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 19th when we started with autopsies. And we worked with each body that was placed on the table. And there was a team who also worked with bodies in the morgue. These are analyses that are carried out in a very simple way, and I think that in a short space of time the investigation or the analyses was carried out on all the samples taken from hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I also understand that fingerprint samples were taken from the bodies to assist in the process of identification; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tips of the fingers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were the fingerprint samples also taken on the 19th of January?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fingerprints were taken later, after the nitrate tests had been carried out in order not to create a disturbance or to affect the particles. That means that these tests were not carried out simultaneously. The paraffin test was done first, and then the fingerprints were taken in order to identify them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm only asking were -- I realise that the two tests were not done simultaneously, but I'm simply trying to clarify: Were the two tests done on the same day or were the fingerprints taken a long time after?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a long time subsequently. When I say "quite a long time," I mean five to six days after the paraffin test was performed on the hands and the area below the elbow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show a little bit more of video, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is some more video provided by Judge Marinkovic. And this is, according to Judge Marinkovic, the weapons that were collected at Racak on the 15th of January, 1999. Weapons and ammunition. We see hand grenades. Then we start to see a number of automatic rifles. You see there's quite a few rifles there. I think that's enough. Now, Professor Dobricanin, we've already discussed, or you have already discussed that the so-called paraffin test is not a perfect test for indications of the presence of gunpowder, and I just wanted to ask you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that -- and of course the purpose of all your work is to try to provide as much information as possible to the legal authorities as precisely as possible so that they may be able to make their decisions about the events in Racak; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I'm trying to understand, then, is you had the fingerprints available, or someone had the fingerprints from these bodies. Did anybody ever test these automatic rifles that were lined up so carefully for the presence of the fingerprints of any of the victims from Racak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you see, if the purpose of this exercise was to get to the truth, eventually find the truth as clearly, precisely, as objectively as possible, wouldn't it have been an obvious and a relatively easy procedure just to see if any of the fingerprints from the victims at Racak were also present on any of these automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is beyond my scope of work. I suppose that perhaps that should have been done. Whether it was done I don't know, and I can't tell you anything further. I saw the weapons later. Now, whether any fingerprints were taken or not, I really don't know that. This is really for the criminal investigation department and other organs; that is not my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, even if it is beyond the scope of your work, if we can just continue this conversation in your role as a citizen. We know that there are at least concerns about the reliability of the so-called paraffin test. Wouldn't it have been a much more precise and final way of determining whether the persons who died at Racak had fired any of those weapons simply by comparing the fingerprints? Just as a citizen. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be one of the pieces of information that could be used for those purposes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or the Republic of Serbia had really wanted to demonstrate the truth about what had happened at Racak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I think you're becoming a little argumentative there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move to the other two factors that you mentioned last week, Professor Dobricanin; the dark coloured clothing as well as the different bullet paths that were found on the victims, and to do that I'm going to have to ask for the patience of everyone in this courtroom as I fumble through a number of exhibits, but I'm going to try to do this as efficiently and as quickly as I can. If we --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like the usher's assistance, perhaps, to place part of Helena Ranta's report on the ELMO, which I have to find. If we turn to appendix 2 of Dr. Ranta's report, and page 9 of appendix 2, we're going to see three bodies. And perhaps page 9 could be placed on the ELMO. You will see there are page numbers in the corner there, so if you could place page 9 on the ELMO, please. Make it easier than using the ERN number, so it should be quicker. For some reason I'm not seeing this. Now it should work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, if you could take a look at this, please. These are the bodies of the three Metushi brothers who were found in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And for the Trial Chamber's edification, this picture is located in what is referred to normally as crime location 2, scene 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And behind me, Professor Dobricanin, I have a large poster, and I'd like to somehow make it visible at least to the Trial Chamber, and to you as well, if we can - I'm going to take my earphones off now - so that you are able to visualise the particular part of Racak where these photographs were taken and where these bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if you would prefer simply to break right now so I don't waste any of the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's a convenient time. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before Mr. Saxon resumes, Your Honour, one matter to raise. I've now been able to look at the issue concerning the further Jasovic material that in fact relates to 57 witness statements. I've had an opportunity to reflect on legal argument which I would like to bring to the attention of Your Honours at an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. We'll hear them later. Continue, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, to your right there is a large poster there on the stand, and just to help keep you and other people in the courtroom oriented I want to go over a few things about it. This is simply an aerial photograph of the Racak area with certain -- with certain locations and landmarks marked on. You will see, Professor Dobricanin, that there's a series of numbers going from 1 to 13 at different points around the village of Racak and in the hills, the hillsides above the village, and these numbers simply refer to what we've been calling in this courtroom different crime locations and different scenes within those locations simply because all of the persons who died at Racak in 1999 did not die in a single place. They died in roughly 13 separate areas in the environs of Racak, and so that's what those numbers represent. You also see some landmarks that you may recall from your visit to the village. For example, there is a black square you'll see on the lower left-hand corner of the poster, with an arrow pointing to a hillside, and that marks the site of the so-called KLA bunker, which I believe you saw when you were walking around Racak. There is also a small flag closer below in the village itself which marks the spot of the so-called headquarters of the KLA unit that was based in Racak, and I believe you visited that house as well. So those are there just to keep yourself and myself and everyone else oriented as we discuss some of the victims of the 15th of January. If you could, please, Professor Dobricanin, take a look at the photograph that is on the projector right now, and you'll see it's a photograph of three bodies. Before we begin, I need -- I should ask you, have you seen such photographs previously? These are photographs of the bodies as they were found in situ after the events of 15 January. Have you seen such photographs before?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't had an opportunity of seeing this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We see in this photograph three bodies. They are the -- they are the three Metushi brothers; Sabri Metushi, also known as Sabri Syla, Arif Metushi, and Haki Metushi. And I would like to review some of the findings of the Finnish forensic experts regarding the autopsies that were done on these three men, if we may. Perhaps if this photograph could be removed and we're first going to refer to the body in the middle is referred to as RA37. That is Mr. Sabri Metushi. And I have another photograph here, and perhaps just to save time I'll simply hand it to Mr. Prendergast. You can use my copy. Place this on the ELMO for everyone to see. And you can see there, Professor Dobricanin, this was a photograph taken during the autopsy of Mr. Sabri Syla, and what we see in the upper photograph here, if you agree, we see the entrance -- we see two entrance wounds for bullets, and then if we go down and look at the lower photograph, we see what appears to be sort of a, if I can call it that, sort of a joint exit wound from the top of the foot. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I describing it correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I remember this case, in fact. I think I remember it, judging by some of the elements there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I realise that I'm very much of a layman. If we can remove that photograph now, please. And if we take a look, RA38 in the first photograph that I showed you of the three bodies in situ was brother Arif Metushi. And I will show another photograph from the Finnish team that is a sketch. Now, we see that according to the results of the autopsy performed, that this man was struck multiple times by gunshots and that the gunshots came from behind him, behind Mr. Metushi, and below him. Is that a fair representation, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the sketch, yes. But there were lateral wounds, number V, for instance, coming in laterally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we can also see what appears -- I guess what you would call a lateral wound, number IV, through the fingers. Is that also correct, a bit more lateral?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And if we could remove that photograph as well. That sketch, I should say. And we'll look at a photograph of Haki Metushi, who was RA39 in the autopsy protocols and is the brother lowest down in this area. And I'd like to put this sketch, if I may, on the ELMO. Again we see that Mr. Haki Metushi was hit by more than one bullet. We see down below it looks like in Mr. Metushi's left leg, it looks like he received a bullet wound just below the knee. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It resembles an injury, and I have no reason to disbelieve it, but maybe it was during the fighting, during fleeing, or any other operation, but they were inflicted more or less at the same time. Let me just intervene. This is nothing separate, special, if that's what you meant. Here the directions of the channels are quite different, or tracks are quite different, and I assumed you noticed that. We have them coming in from the top, from the bottom, from right to left under an angle, from left to right under an angle, then one again -- some again from quite another direction. So this is a perfect illustration of what I was saying the other day; that there are different directions, different tracks, different bullet paths, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Professor, and that's what I want to ask you about. Another thing you said the other day was that one of the reasons why you believe that these persons were killed during some kind of combat is because most of the wounds were found either in the upper body or in the head, which would indicate that they were standing in trenches at the time. And here, for example, we see in this sketch we see someone who was shot in the left lower leg; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I showed you a few minutes ago the brother of this -- of the person represented in this sketch, who was Sabri Metushi, who was shot actually through the sole of his foot twice. So such wounds would not be consistent with someone standing in a trench, would they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you thinking? What's on your mind? I will be happy to give you an explanation if His Honour Judge Robinson will allow me to try and explain something with respect to this particular case. An injury in the -- on the neck, under number I, was inflicted from this direction, top to bottom. Can you assume that this man was in some form of trench when he was shot from this position? The left lateral wound is now from the opposite, reverse direction. The injury in the -- on the right thigh a little to the back and to the side, whereas on the right-hand side they are all right to left under an angle. Now, can you picture the following situation: I could give you a concrete answer if we had been able to go into Racak and see the bodies in situ. If he had tried to flee, there is an uphill slope, and that he was hit, which shows us the injury on the left lower arm, the left thigh and these other injuries. They are parallel channel directions or track directions. And in this way we can explain it very simply. But I cannot accept any kind of explanation outside what we did during the autopsies, because once again we -- let me say we were not allowed, and the Judge and I was a professional, to go in situ, to the site where the bodies were actually found. These are post festum findings, four days later when we came upon the bodies in Racak and we started conducting the autopsies. Then we have this. I and my colleagues would know exactly whether the bodies were found in the spot they were killed, whether they had been moved, whether they had been dressed again, and so on and so forth. We would know that exactly had we been allowed to enter onto the site. I am sorry for being a little more lengthy in my answer but I had to explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, you say the injuries to the lower part of the body could be explained if they were fleeing up -- up a hill.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, yes. Yes, Your Honour. If I might be allowed to add, Your Honour, another example with respect to the first sketch. I wasn't given the chance of saying anything there. On those bodies, on the bodies of the two men on an uphill slope, you find the caps in the position in which I indicated on Friday and said that it was impossible to find caps in that position, which means that the body had been manipulated with. And I will tell you one more thing: If you are hit on an uphill slope, there's absolutely no chance that you will stay there. The body will topple and roll down the hill and find itself ending up in a quite different location from where it was hit. And here all the bodies were turned head upwards, head towards the hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, is it likely that in an incident such as what happened at Racak, that when people were killed survivors or whoever happens to come by and sees the bodies, it's not uncommon, is it, that they might turn over a body to see who this person is, whether or not they are still alive? That's not uncommon, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not uncommon if we're dealing with an individual killing. But if we're dealing with a mass killing during combat, rare would be the person after so much shooting who would dare run up to see what was going on. You know, there is justified fear that there are still parties in the conflict there and that you could lose your head very easily perhaps later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, didn't you say about one minute ago that you couldn't comment on matters outside of your autopsies? Because then how do you explain your last response?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that you asked me as a man who doesn't have to deal in forensics. It's the explanation of an ordinary citizen. My behaviour, how I would behave in a situation like that or anybody else outside forensic medicine. Your question was outside the realm of forensic medicine, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your comment of last week that the fact that bodies have wounds on the upper part of the body indicates that the deceased persons were fighting in trenches, that is also outside the realm of forensic medicine, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That falls only partially within the realm of forensic medicine. I didn't say that none of them had injuries and wounds on the lower part of the body. I said that they were mostly in the upper half of the body, the upper torso, whereas wounds like this can be administered in trench fighting and in other types of fighting depending on the configuration of the terrain where all this happens. This is a hilly terrain so the bullet path directions can take different courses. So that is altogether outside the realm of what I know as forensic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the report of a forensic pathologist named Eric Baccard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never heard of him. He didn't work with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so you know, he presented a report in this case back in April of 2002, and in his report he reported that 18 per cent of the injuries Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that were recorded during these autopsies of the Racak victims were found on the lower limbs. So that's almost 1 in 5. That's almost 20 per cent. A significant number of injuries found on the lower limbs of the victims. Do you have any comment to make about that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That means that four-fifths were found in the upper half of the body. And that's what I said. I said that the majority of the wounds, four-fifths are a considerable amount, more than one-fifth, were in the upper half of the body; the thorax, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I now would like to show a drawing from Dr. Helena Ranta's report. And it's also from appendix 2, and it's also related to the same particular crime scene from the Racak area, which was crime location 2, scene 2, in the case of Metushi brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If this could be placed on the -- on the ELMO, please. Let me just read out the ERN number: K0202405.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about this. Professor Dobricanin, this photograph was made in March of 2000 when the Finnish forensic team had an opportunity to return to the Racak site, and they went to several of the crime locations, and with the help of a metal detector they searched for bullet casings and bullets or the remains of bullets in relation to the locations where were different bodies were found. And this particular photograph shows the positions of what I have referred to as victim 37, who would be here in this photograph 13; victim 10 who was RA39 from your forensic autopsy reports; and the victim that was further up the hill, the white marker that says 7014, was actually victim number 38 in the work that you did. But we see behind the markers were the bodies -- behind these white markers we see a series of blue markers. Each blue marker represents the spot where a bullet or bullet fragment was found in the soil along that hillside. And I can show you as well another photograph, but before I do, would the presence of bullets in the soil so close behind a spot where those three bodies were found indicate that those men were shot where they were found?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me something to which I cannot give you an answer to for the following reasons: How come and who knows that this was truly the location if the investigation by the legal Yugoslav authorities was not conducted on the day of the event? That's the first point. Secondly, it is absolutely possible to feign this in any part of Kosovo and Metohija, any village, and then say that you found projectiles in the soil. A projectile, a bullet that has not been identified ballistically and not treated ballistically and that has not been compared with the weapon from which it was allegedly shot, there is absolutely no possibility for that projectile to be any kind of proof or evidence whatsoever. These very indistinct photographs that you're showing here, I really cannot comment upon them. All I can tell you is what you ask me, if you could find that anywhere at Kosovo, there was so much shooting in Kosovo that you can find rounds, bullet casings or anything, as many as you like anywhere. So if you don't have actual facts and figures where it came from, there's no point in you asking me this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to try to give you a few more facts, Professor Dobricanin. I simply asked your opinion. I'm not trying to be difficult. If you could keep your answers short so we could move along a bit more quickly. I think we've all heard you. Let me show you my next photograph. This is also from Helena Ranta's report. It's photograph number 14 in appendix 2, ERN K0202411. I'm wondering if we could move that photograph a little bit more in the other direction. Yes, yes. Back to the left now. Perfect. Thank you. Again, Professor Dobricanin, in March of 2000 when the Finnish forensic team went back to the site, not only do they find bullets or bullet fragments in the hillside up on the left of this photograph but they also found a number of cartridge cases in the debris and in the silt and the dirt you see down in the lower right-hand corner there. And every small white square, or rectangle, I should say, represents a spot where a cartridge case was found. Now, combining the fact that we have photographs of bodies in situ up on the left side of the hillside, we have bullets found embedded in the soil behind where those bodies were found, and we have cartridge cases down below to the right, and some of those -- some of the wounds suffered by the deceased in this scene were received from below and behind, in your opinion, whether professional or as a citizen, do you think we can conclude that perhaps the persons who did the firing were down in this area in the right hand -- lower right-hand portion of the photograph, firing up towards the left where the bodies were found? Can we possibly conclude that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me to give an affirmative answer, then I would be a great layman in terms of forensic medicine, because each site you can do anything you like along this, feign this. We found a large number of casings. Does that mean that the casings there are relevant whereas in another place by the graveside they're irrelevant? This is a hill. You can do what you like. You can show anything, that the shooting came from any direction you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how can you do that scientifically, Professor Dobricanin? How can you show that anything you like, that shootings came from any particular direction? If you have an autopsy done of the body, if you have a study done of the bullet paths, how can you possibly do whatever you like? For example, in this photograph we see a tree. You're not suggesting that someone could have feigned these results so that cartridges would have been found up on the top of that tree, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is possible, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, you're saying that this is part of Dr. Helena Ranta's report?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. This is found in appendix 2 to Dr. Ranta's report, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have it in as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, you do, Your Honour. It is Exhibit 156, tab 12. I'm sorry if I didn't make that clear previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, where is the evidence that the bullets were found in soil near to where the bodies were?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: From Dr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the report as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In Dr. Ranta's report, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the photographs that I've just shown you and discussed with you, Professor Dobricanin, do you see any evidence there that the men who died were firing back at the men who killed them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who could say anything like this. On the basis of this photograph you can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can't see any cartridge cases marked up on the left-hand side close to the bodies, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be a mark for anything. I don't see cases. Possibly there were, but I don't see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you -- are you doubting the integrity of the final report of the Finnish team? Is that what you're suggesting, that they had faked this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if our team was prohibited from entering the village on the 15th, 16th, and 17th, then in my opinion something must have happened there. Why were we otherwise forbidden from entering? The only person who on behalf of the state authorities was authorised to carry out investigation was Judge Danica Marinkovic. Had we entered Racak on that day, we would have found this or something else. On the basis of something that was done a year later, you cannot establish where the bodies were at the moment when they were killed and where the casings were found. You probably know it is possible to doctor a scene any way you want. I'm not saying that that's what our colleagues did, but somebody else could have done it and then brought them to have a look at that. Why didn't they call us when all of this was being done so we could be together on the scene?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Judge Danica Marinkovic and her authority that she had. Did Judge Marinkovic need to seek the authority of the district prosecutor to carry out her investigation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment when I went there, it was the deputy public prosecutor, district prosecutor who was there, and the deputy district prosecutor has all possible powers in this respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Judge Marinkovic have to seek the permission of the public prosecutor to interview witnesses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did it together. They did everything on the request of the public prosecutor's office in Pristina. That's what she did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to -- I just want to make one more point about this particular photograph provided to us by the Finnish team, and that is simply this: Also included in the report in appendix 2, we're told that all of the cartridge cases that are represented by these rectangles in the lower right-hand corner, they came from two weapons, and each of the -- the cartridge cases, the -- represented ammunition of only two different brands. One was the Igman brand, and the other was a brand known as PPU. These are brands of ammunition manufactured in Serbia, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is Igman ammunition, then that's not in Serbia. That's in Bosnia-Herzegovina. PPU means Prvi Partizan Uzice. This is a factory from the town of Uzice that manufactures ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these two kinds of ammunition are used by police and military forces of Yugoslavia and Serbia, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only they but also everyone who took part in this war; the Albanians, members of the KLA. Everybody used both. Actually, the Albanians used this ammunition which was in the Territorial Defence arms depots that had been looted, and they also used Chinese ammunition that they brought from Albania. Of course, the military mostly used PPU and I don't know what else, but manufactured in Serbia, I think. Or, rather, it wasn't the military, it was the police. I am sorry, I made a mistake. But I don't know what the army used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give me your views as a citizen regarding this scene if not as a forensic professional. We have three men. They're older. They're lying dead on a hillside. They're dressed in civilian clothes. Some of their wounds but not all of them came from below and behind. According to one group of forensic experts, there are bullets found in the soil close to where their bodies were found, and there are cartridge casings found down below. Is it possible -- or would it be possible to conclude, or would one -- maybe better put, would one possibility be, based on this evidence, that these three men were murdered? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if we had attended the investigation while the bodies were still there where they fell could we come to a relevant conclusion. Such conclusions can only be made once there is a complete reconstruction on the basis of the initial investigation, with photographs of the scene and bodies on the scene and with further examinations. Bullet path directions are not only part of the work of forensic experts but also ballistics experts. I do not understand why they did not allow us access immediately or at least in 2000 when this mini reconstruction, if I can call it that, was conducted. Why could we not take part in it when we did the autopsies together on the bodies of the persons found in Racak?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, are you aware of any reports or records, documentation that indicate whether weapons were found in the spots where bodies were found at Racak such as these three bodies?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I have no such reports or was I interested in that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move to a different scene, different crime location. And just to keep you oriented, Professor Dobricanin, and everyone else, the scene I'm going to discuss now is crime location 4, scene 9, which on that poster there is a bit higher up on the poster than the crime scene location that we -- that we just discussed. If you'll bear with me for one moment. I want to show you -- we don't have an in situ photograph of the bodies for this crime location, however, we do have some autopsy photographs, and I'd like to discuss one or two of them with you, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I could -- I'm sorry, Mr. Prendergast, I have to call you over here again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a photograph of one of the persons who died at this scene. This is a boy named Halim Zeqiri, and he was 14 when he died in Racak on the 15th of January, and he received one bullet wound. It was from the back and exited through his neck. So that is the exit wound we see there, isn't it, Professor Dobricanin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be seen here, right here, this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be seen very well here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me -- just to help you and help everyone else, let me just show you the entry wound.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be seen very well here, but it's marked, so I assume that that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So again we have someone who was shot from behind and below. This was -- can we see the other photograph, please? Halim was 14 at the time. Professor Dobricanin, do you think it's possible that this boy was simply an innocent civilian?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you draw that conclusion. This is a 14-year-old boy. Among the Albanians, boys of that age are mature. Many of them carried weapons. And this positioning of the wound from the bottom upwards shows that he was on a hillside too. That was the entire terrain. It was on the slopes above the village. So it is possible to be killed in any spot. This is a typical bullet path for a person who is climbing uphill, or which would be very unlikely -- I have to explain this. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I'm sorry, perhaps my question was not clear. I will rephrase it. I simply asked: Is it possible this boy was simply an innocent civilian? Do you think it's possible?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I have no grounds for answering that question. If you're only referring to his age, that doesn't mean anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was simply whether it's possible. I wasn't asking you to draw any final conclusions.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have answered that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me go back to another point. You mentioned that this is a typical bullet path for a person who was climbing uphill. Wouldn't it also be a typical bullet path for someone who is fleeing uphill, running away?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say to you whether the person was running away or moving slowly. There are no characteristics on the bodily wounds that could indicate the speed at which a person moves at the moment when he or she is hit by a bullet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think I'll leave that question for now, Professor. This boy, Halim Zeqiri, his father was also killed on the 15th of January, and his mother and his sister -- his sister were wounded and were taken to the hospital for treatment. Did you ever speak with them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I never came to Racak again after the 18th of January, and I never encountered any resident of the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wouldn't it have been one way to clarify the events of that day simply by speaking to wounded survivors who could tell you what they saw and experienced on that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that is not within the scope of my work. If anybody was supposed to speak to them, it was the investigating judge. And secondly, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. if they were transferred to the hospital in Pristina, perhaps the investigating judge could have talked to them. However, as far as I know, they had their local medical service where the wounded were treated. I don't know exactly in which village, but it was somewhere in the immediate vicinity of the village of Racak. They had their own doctors, and they had their own medical support for their units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were working on the autopsies for this medicolegal investigation, did you -- were you given access to any records regarding the wounded, the wounded survivors?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, we'll stop in five minutes to hear the legal submissions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, Professor? Were you given access to any records regarding the wounded, the wounded survivors?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no documentation. I have not seen any documentation. I would like to stress once again that these persons were not treated in the Pristina hospital at all but at this other medical centre. There are no records of them. I would have had to know because somebody from surgery would have certainly called me to tell me someone was there. They usually call us when there are severely wounded persons there so that we could come and have a look. I don't think that any one of them was treated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, is it possible that the survivors were treated in the hospital in Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no hospital in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we had a nine-year-old boy who was shot in the leg on the 15th of January and received treatment in some kind of medical facility in Stimlje. Efrem Salmi [phoen], I believe is his name.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think this was in Stimlje. It is certain that the wounded Albanians from Racak could not reach Stimlje. This was quite a bit of police still there, but it's quite possible that he was in the village clinic either in Racak or on the periphery of Stimlje near Racak, Rance, Petrovo Selo and the other villages that were there. As far as I know, I heard from my colleagues, my Albanian colleagues, that every one of these units had this kind of medical support, and before the war every village had a clinic of its own to treat the residents of the village. These persons, these doctors who were in these villages were only Albanians because these were exclusively Albanian villages. It is possible that some kind of a hospital had been set up there, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to, and I know we're short of time, but you made a reference to "every one of these units had this kind of medical support." Which units are you referring to? Are you referring to KLA units?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the KLA units for sure. And if you're asking me about our units, they also had their own medical corps. When I say "our," I'm saying the police of Serbia. Don't think that I belong to these units. In any kind of troops there is also a medical corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that this victim, Halim Beqiri, then, was a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be a good point for me to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Professor, we are going to hear some legal arguments. I think it would probably be more convenient for you to just stay for the five, ten minutes. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The issue concerns the Jasovic statements which were served on the Prosecution very recently. That's a file that consists of 57 further witness statements sought to be produced through the witness Jasovic. Those are witness statements deriving from the time period 1998 to 1999, and indicate activities of the KLA. Within those statements there are further names as well as a repetition of the names already mentioned within the tabs of tab 45, I think it is, to 53 of Exhibit 293, which were the witness statements adduced through the witness Marinkovic, which again indicate that a number of those deceased mentioned in Schedule A of the indictment were connected with the KLA or have been referred to as having connections with the KLA through sources who were interviewed by the police in that period of 1998 to 1999. It comes down to about 30 of those names in Schedule A fall into that category. So they are identified in witness statements taken by the witness Jasovic in the period 1998 to 1999 as having been involved with the KLA. This is very different from the Barney Kelly, Kevin Curtis evidence sought to be relied on by the Prosecution, who were Prosecution investigators who had summarised the contents of a series of witness statements taken over a period of time from 1999 to later periods, and the Prosecutor sought to include that evidence from those witnesses as summarising witnesses, and as the Trial Chamber knows, the Appeals Chamber found against that practice using the investigators to summarise the contents of the witness statements. The Prosecutor didn't want to use the full witness statements but wanted to use those investigators as summarising witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if we were to admit the statements, would you not agree that the declarants should be brought for cross-examination, should be available for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can assist the Court, this was material produced at the time, contemporaneous material within the files of the law enforcement agencies, prosecutor services, and was not material that was created or produced for this litigation. So it stands apart from material that has been made by one party for the purposes of the proceeding. It is material that is part of what was happening at the time. This case concerns the criminal responsibility of the accused and goes to the issue of his state of mind. If there are official records at the time that have not been created for the issue that we're concerned with in this trial and that they are within the system of the law enforcement agencies, it is right to say that the accused would be entitled to rely upon the content of that information to prove matters relevant to the issue concerning his state of mind. The issue here is what the accused knew or ought to have known, what he was led to believe, what were the facts at his disposal. That has been a line that has been cross-examined upon by the Prosecution. If this officer is someone who in the course of his duties was able to prepare a number of original exhibits, original material on issues unconnected with the accused at the time but for a completely different reason that indicate the extent of the issue concerning the power, the control, what was being done, the acts and conduct of the KLA, that is material, in our submission, that this accused would be entitled to rely upon in his Defence if it proves an issue in his favour. And it's very different from the other material. These proceedings would not have been designed for him to call 80 such witnesses if they were available and willing to be called to give evidence about those matters, which is really the way Mr. Nice put his submission this morning. What is important here, what this goes to is what was known within the system. What had been produced in the system that was nothing to do with these proceedings, entirely independent, and part of the general information involved at the time. We have a parallel: The Prosecution relied on the statements produced through Captain Dragan. The Court will remember he gave evidence. His real name was Vasiljkovic. He produced -- the Prosecution sought to rely upon about 10.000 pages of CD-ROM through him, which were the records of soldiers who had been injured and had received support from a foundation. Within those records there was a statement of where the soldier originated from, from Serbia or elsewhere, who he had served with as a soldier, and what his injuries were. This was objected to by the accused and the amici curiae, but the evidence was admitted on the basis that it was evidence that had become part of an official record that had been produced, nothing to do with this litigation, but it gave information that the Prosecution was seeking to rely upon not only for the fact of the content but also the truth, and the purpose behind it was to prove that there had been Serbian soldiers involved in the conflict within Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Suppose the accused had sought to produce the witness statements through 92 bis. Would the Prosecution not be entitled to seek to cross-examine the declarants?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 92 bis is not the only -- only route. They're not being called for what they would say now. They're being called -- this evidence is being used for what they said then, and that's the importance of it. What was said at the time, the contemporaneity. Just in the same way as the Prosecutor relied on Exhibit 391, tabs 4 to 8, the Captain Dragan materials, for what was said then to prove an issue that they needed in relation to their case against the accused, this accused, in our submission, would be entitled to use that original evidence. It's original evidence. He's not relying upon it for the statement of the witness. He is relying upon it for what was said and known at that time. They're not coming here as witnesses. That content is being adduced through the witness as exhibit material. And not exhibit material prepared over the weekend, as the Prosecutor has sought to do and would no doubt try to draw a parallel between these instances. That was exhibited -- exhibit material that was prepared before any indictment, completely unrelated to this case and, therefore, falls within that classic material that is admissible in any trial of what original material was in existence at the time, and it's highly relevant to this accused's Defence as to his state of mind. If there were a vast body of material within the archives of the Kosovan MUP declaring the contrary to this kind of material, no doubt the Prosecutor would have sought to rely upon it in prosecution of the accused. And the way the Appeals Chamber dealt with these issues, and the Trial Chamber, was not to close down the use of original material that may have been taken in statement form. It wasn't being exclusive in the use of Rule 92 bis as applying merely to statements. 92 bis applies to statements taken for the proceedings, for Court statements taken through an officer of the Court, and therein lies its restriction. This is being relied upon as exhibit material to show what was out there, what was in existence at the time that forms a bedrock to the Defence of the accused. A very, very different set of circumstances to the material that the Prosecutor has sought to rely on in his prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks. Let me just hear Mr. Nice very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, to deal with this it may take a couple of minutes, and I haven't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We just -- I don't want to trespass on the time of the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I also need to ask something of you of an administrative nature before we close today, and it's this: If Helena Ranta is available tomorrow - and I don't know whether she is - might it be the case the Court would want to hear from her? She had originally been called by the Court. If so, I will convey the request to her. If the Court doesn't envisage that it might want to hear from her, then -- and if she's otherwise free tomorrow, then we'll make our own decision whether to inconvenience her further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For my own part, no, I don't wish to hear from her. We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Obviously, we need to let her know this afternoon because she's taken two days out of her schedule in order to make herself available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think we'll have to continue this tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think so because I'm afraid that I don't really quite understand my learned friend's submissions. What I would be grateful to know, if the Court can ask the accused one question, is if, as Mr. Kay says, and these are documents are all fresh to me and without any translation, but if these documents suggest that names on Schedule A are shown to be members of the KLA, whatever Mr. Kay's argument, is the accused seeking to rely on this document to prove that people killed in the Racak incident were members of the KLA? Because if he is, then that's different from Mr. Kay's argument and I need to be able to address that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I don't know if the Court will feel able to help me with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll continue this debate tomorrow morning. It's almost time, and we don't wish to trespass on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'd be grateful if you would give some thought to this: There are two trials in this court, and they both involve the same witness or potential witness. The Prosecution position in relation to that witness, I understand, is entirely different in the other case from the position it appears to be taking in relation to the witness in this case. I'll be interested to hear you further tomorrow when we can continue this on whether that's an appropriate position for the Prosecution to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a matter I've already considered and I'll return to it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 13th day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
